catalog_quote: 1. Stress assignment. The rules assigning stress to syllables are the fundamental determinants of whether the syllable will contain a vowel of predictable or unpredictable quality. As in Northern Straits and other Salishan languages stress assignment is generally morphologically conditioned--certain suffixes attract stress. In Klallam as in Saanich there is a tendency to penultimate stress other things being equal. I leave a fuller description of Klallam stress placement for a later study. It suffices here simply to say that primary stress is assigned to one of the vowels of the fully derived word.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (Montler 1998, ICSNL 33, author's open PDF from montler.net; text present, extracted with extracted text). The quoted passage is on the 4th PDF page (footer page number '4'; the compiler locator says 'p. 3 = 4th PDF page' -- the printed footer is 4, trivial), under the numbered list of processes, item '1. Stress assignment.' It reads word for word: 'The rules assigning stress to syllables are the fundamental determinants of whether the syllable will contain a vowel of predictable or unpredictable quality. As in Northern Straits and other Salishan languages stress assignment is generally morphologically conditioned--certain suffixes attract stress. In Klallam as in Saanich there is a te…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per (fully derived) word; its position is determined morphologically -- roots and suffixes differ in whether they take/attract stress (Montler 2015 Sec. 31.1: weak stems shift the accented vowel rightward under suffixation, strong stems keep it, zero stems have no stressable vowel and a stressed suffix or inserted schwa carries stress; Sec. 40.1: suffixes like causative -istxw take stress from the root, whose vowel then reduces to schwa) -- with a default tendency toward the penultimate syllable when morphology does not decide. Unstressed full vowels reduce to schwa and unstressed schwa deletes, so stress is marked lexically with an acute in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in the 1998 paper ('primary stress is assigned to one of the vowels'); the 2015 grammar (Sec. 41.6) notes the particle ay'ngen carries its own stress without removing the host word's stress, otherwise one accent per stressable word.
new_statements.exceptions: Montler 2015 Sec. 40.1: seven stems keep their stress when causative -istxw is added; Sec. 31.1: no way to tell weak from strong t-stems by shape, 'most other stems are weak stems'; particles (u 'question', ya? 'past') never stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'primary stress is assigned to one of the vowels of the fully derived word' (1998); grammar: only 'stressable words' (verbs, nouns, adjectives, numbers, focus pronouns, intensifiers) bear an accent, short grammatical particles never do. Pitch and length not distinctive (Montler 2004).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Klallam proper (clal1241; Elwha/Jamestown/Port Gamble speakers, Montler's fieldwork mainly Lower Elwha and Becher Bay). Montler explicitly compares with Saanich/Northern Straits (stra1244), which is a separate language already in the catalog.

new_statements.quote: Under non-primary stress vowels optionally reduce to shwa. Unstressed shwa has a wide variation of phonetic qualities many of which overlap with phonetic variants of other vowels under non-primary stress. [...] The assumption is then, no vowel other than shwa occurs unstressed. Since primary stress can occur only once in a word (few exceptions have been noted, i.e., /xáápuʔ/ 'basket grass (unidentified)'), all occurrences of unstressed shwa are predictable and therefore phonetic. The result is that a word will contain only one systematic vowel phoneme.
new_statements.citation: Fleisher, Mark Stewart. 1976. Clallam: A Study in Coast Salish Ethnolinguistics. PhD dissertation, Washington State University.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 5 Phonology, 'Phonological Rules' and 'Additional Considerations', pp. 151-154 (PDF pages 164-167); deciding sentences pp. 153-154. Verified against the page scan, not only the scanned layer.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: I re-extracted PDF pages 164-167 (printed pp. 151-154) with extracted text: the whole quoted passage is on p. 153 ('Additional Considerations') running onto p. 154, verbatim once the letter-spaced scanned is collapsed: 'Under non-primary stress vowels optionally reduce to shwa. Unstressed shwa has a wide variation of phonetic qualities many of which overlap with phonetic variants of other vowels under non-primary stress.. The assumption is then, no vowel other than shwa occurs unstressed. Since primary stress can occur only once in a word (few exceptions have been noted, i.e., /xaapu?/ 'basket grass (unidentified)'), all occurrences of unstressed shwa are predictable and therefore phonetic.…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Montler 1998: stress assignment is morphologically conditioned) and adds only domain and culminativity detail: exactly one primary stress per word (rare exceptions), reduction of non-primary-stress vowels to schwa, and a tense/lax alternation under primary stress. It supplies no placement rule, so it neither confirms nor disputes the morphological-conditioning reading; downgrade to 'silent' if only placement statements count.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dissertation gives no rule for where word stress falls. It states only that primary stress is culminative (one primary stress per word, with rare exceptions such as /xáápuʔ/ which carries two acute marks), that vowels under non-primary stress optionally reduce to schwa and are neutralized, that vowels are tense under primary stress before back obstruents and affricates (rule 5.9, p. 152), and that a glottal stop drops between unstressed vowels (rule 5.7, p. 151). Stress is marked with an acute in cited forms (e.g. /pehéqʷ/ 'nighthawk', /spáʔxʷəŋ/ 'fog', /ʔáplus/ 'apple', /qʷəʔúys/ 'juicy') but no placement principle, weight, or morphological conditioning is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Distinguishes 'primary' from 'non-primary' stress and uses a [-1 Stress] feature in rules 5.7 and 5.9, implying more than one degree of stress, but says nothing about where secondary stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: 'few exceptions have been noted' to one-primary-stress-per-word, with the single example /xáápuʔ/ 'basket grass (unidentified)' (pp. 153-154).
new_statements.identity_note: Fleisher's data come from Lower Elwha Klallam speakers (Washington State; he reports Lower Elwha informants, ch. 1 p. 6) and he treats Clallam as a dialect of Straits Salish. Same variety as the catalog's Montler sources (Klallam, Olympic Peninsula).

sources.note: Pedagogical: stress is written with an acute on every stressable word (verbs, nouns, adjectives, numbers, focus pronouns, intensifiers); particles never stressed; stressed vowel louder and longer.
